3 min read 1 hour ago -- Day 4: Why JavaScript Exists — And Why It’s More Than Just “Making Websites Interactive” Press enter or click to view image in full size Yesterday, I revisited HTML and CSS and finally understood their individual responsibilities. That naturally led me to another question. If HTML creates the structure and CSS controls the presentation, why do we need JavaScript? Like many beginners, I used to think JavaScript was simply used to make websites interactive. Buttons click. Menus open. Animations happen. That explanation isn’t wrong — but it’s incomplete. The more I revisited the fundamentals, the more I realised that JavaScript isn’t just about interactions. It’s about adding behaviour and decision-making to a webpage. HTML Knows What Exists HTML tells the browser what elements exist on the page. For example,

Welcome

The browser understands that there’s a heading, an input field, and a button. But HTML cannot answer questions like: • What happens when the button is clicked? • Is the email valid? • Should the user be redirected after logging in? • Should an error message appear? HTML simply describes the structure. CSS Knows How It Looks CSS controls presentation. It decides: • Colors • Fonts • Layout • Animations • Responsive Design But CSS also cannot make decisions. It cannot validate a form or fetch data from an API. JavaScript Knows What Should Happen This was probably my biggest realisation today. JavaScript gives a webpage the ability to think and respond. For example, let age = 20;if (age >= 18) { console.log("Eligible to Vote"); } This isn’t about making a button interactive. It’s about making a decision based on data. JavaScript introduces concepts like: • Variables • Conditions • Functions • Loops • Objects • Events These concepts allow applications to react differently depending on user input or application state. JavaScript Connects the User and the Application Another perspective that made everything click for me was this: A user interacts with the UI. JavaScript receives that interaction. It processes the logic. Then it decides how the UI should change. For example, during login: • User enters an email and password. • JavaScript validates the inputs. • It sends an API request. • It receives the server’s response. • It updates the UI by showing either an error or navigating the user to the dashboard. Without JavaScript, the webpage would display information — but it couldn’t respond intelligently to user actions. Why Frontend Developers Spend So Much Time Learning JavaScript One thing I misunderstood earlier was thinking that frontend development was mostly about designing screens. After revisiting the fundamentals, I realised that a large part of frontend development is actually writing application logic. Questions like: • Should this button be disabled? • Is the user logged in? • Should this component be visible? • Is the entered password strong enough? • What should happen if an API request fails? These aren’t styling problems. They’re JavaScript problems. The UI simply reflects the decisions made by the application’s logic. My Biggest Realisation I used to think learning JavaScript meant memorising syntax. Today, I see it differently. JavaScript isn’t just another programming language added to the browser. It’s the language responsible for turning a static webpage into an application that can process data, make decisions, and respond to users. That’s probably why every modern frontend framework — whether React, Angular, Vue, or Svelte — is fundamentally built around JavaScript. Frameworks may simplify development, but the logic behind them is still JavaScript. What’s Next? Now that I understand why JavaScript exists, it’s finally time to revisit the language itself. I’ll begin with the fundamentals — variables, data types, operators, and conditional statements — not by memorizing syntax, but by understanding how JavaScript thinks and executes code. I’m looking forward to strengthening the foundation before moving back into React. “HTML defines the structure. CSS defines the presentation. JavaScript defines the behaviour and decision-making. Together, they transform a webpage into an application.” If you’re also revisiting software engineering fundamentals, I’d love to have you along on this journey. Feel free to share your thoughts or suggestions in the comments, or reach out to me at urbashijrall3003@gmail.com.
